title: Judges 9:22–33
context: Abimelech rules for three years. Then God sends an evil spirit between him and the men of Shechem, so that the bloodshed of Gideon’s sons will return on those responsible. Shechem turns to banditry and then to Gaal son of Ebed, who mocks Abimelech at a harvest feast in the house of their god. Zebul, Abimelech’s officer in the city, secretly sends word and advises an ambush at dawn.

verses.text: Abimelech was prince over Israel three years.
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech is prince over Israel three years. Arminian readers note the brief duration and see the narrator downplaying his rule, which seems limited in scope despite the phrase “over Israel” in the text.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the narrator gives no sign of God’s approval during these years, only their passing. Both traditions read the short notice as a pause before judgment begins, with the three years marking a limited reign.

verses.text: Then God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem; and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech,
verses.arminianNotes: God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem, and Shechem deals treacherously. Arminian readers often read this as God giving them over to the discord their own sin had already produced, judging them through their choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm that God actively ordained this judgment, governing even evil agents and dispositions while remaining just and not the author of sin. Shared ground: the text presents the spirit as God’s righteous judgment on the guilty (9:24).
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions affirm that God judged Abimelech and Shechem justly and is not the author of sin. Classical Arminian readers generally describe God’s role in terms of permitting and directing evil already chosen by human agents, giving them over to its consequences. Reformed readers generally hold that God ordains and governs such events, including evil agents, so that human wickedness serves His purposes while the guilt remains with the humans. The difference concerns how God’s agency relates to human evil, not whether the judgment was just.

verses.text: that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and that their blood might be laid on Abimelech their brother who killed them, and on the men of Shechem who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.
verses.arminianNotes: The purpose is that the violence done to the seventy sons might return on Abimelech and the men who strengthened his hands. Arminian readers see moral accountability applied to all who freely took part in the massacre.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s justice as precise, bringing blood guilt back on the guilty parties. Both traditions agree that this verse explains the meaning of 9:23: what follows is judgment for bloodshed, not random misfortune.

verses.text: The men of Shechem set an ambush for him on the tops of the mountains, and they robbed all who came along that way by them; and Abimelech was told about it.
verses.arminianNotes: The men of Shechem set ambushes on the mountains and rob travelers, and Abimelech hears of it. Arminian readers see Shechem’s own lawlessness at work, undermining Abimelech’s authority and damaging the region’s trade.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the treachery foretold in 9:23 now takes concrete form. Shared ground: the partnership that began in bloodshed turns to disorder, and the story shows the evil spirit’s effect through ordinary human wrongdoing.

verses.text: Gaal the son of Ebed came with his brothers and went over to Shechem; and the men of Shechem put their trust in him.
verses.arminianNotes: Gaal son of Ebed arrives with his brothers, and Shechem puts its trust in him. Arminian readers note how quickly loyalty shifts in a community that had chosen its king on the basis of kinship and money.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Shechem’s new trust another misplaced reliance, now on Gaal instead of Abimelech. Both traditions read the episode as the beginning of open revolt, showing the instability of power gained by violence.

verses.text: They went out into the field, harvested their vineyards, trod the grapes, celebrated, and went into the house of their god and ate and drank, and cursed Abimelech.
verses.arminianNotes: At the harvest festival, Shechem feasts in the house of their god and curses Abimelech. Arminian readers note that the celebration combines idolatry, drunkenness, and rebellion in a single scene of corporate folly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the house of their god, likely linked to Baal Berith (9:4), is now where Abimelech is cursed. Shared ground: the god that funded Abimelech’s rise now hosts his rejection, a sign of how unstable idolatry is.

verses.text: Gaal the son of Ebed said, “Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Isn’t he the son of Jerubbaal? Isn’t Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem, but why should we serve him?
verses.arminianNotes: Gaal mocks Abimelech as Jerubbaal’s son and urges service to the men of Hamor, father of Shechem. Arminian readers see an appeal to older Canaanite roots in the city (compare Genesis 34), setting Shechemite identity against Abimelech.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that Abimelech, who rose by claiming kinship with Shechem, is now dismissed as an outsider. Both traditions read Gaal’s speech as tribal and political rivalry with no regard for God’s purposes.

verses.text: I wish that this people were under my hand! Then I would remove Abimelech.” He said to Abimelech, “Increase your army and come out!”
verses.arminianNotes: Gaal boasts that if the people were under his hand he would remove Abimelech, and dares him to bring out his army. Arminian readers see a bold, perhaps drunken challenge made at the feast without any real plan behind it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see pride before a fall, a pattern the next scenes will confirm. Shared ground: Gaal’s boast echoes Abimelech’s own grasping for power, and both men will be brought down by the conflict they have stirred up.

verses.text: When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger burned.
verses.arminianNotes: Zebul, the city’s ruler, hears Gaal’s words and burns with anger. Arminian readers note that Zebul, as Abimelech’s officer, remains loyal and becomes the key to Gaal’s defeat through his position in the city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the story’s web of plotting deepen as loyalties divide within Shechem. Both traditions read Zebul’s anger as the trigger for the counterplot, with Shechem’s internal conflict now serving the judgment Jotham foretold.

verses.text: He sent messengers to Abimelech craftily, saying, “Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his brothers have come to Shechem; and behold, they incite the city against you.
verses.arminianNotes: Zebul sends secret word to Abimelech that Gaal is stirring up the city. Arminian readers note the craftiness in the message, part of a story in which deceit and treachery shape every move by every side.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the story shows no righteous party among the main actors. Shared ground: the narrative describes political intrigue without approval, allowing readers to see the moral confusion that follows abandoning God.

verses.text: Now therefore, go up by night, you and the people who are with you, and lie in wait in the field.
verses.arminianNotes: Zebul advises Abimelech to come by night and lie in wait in the field. Arminian readers note the practical military counsel and the way an insider in the city enables the attack on the very people he governs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the plan as one more means in the unfolding judgment, though carried out by people with their own motives. Both traditions read Zebul’s advice as an ordinary act of political loyalty within a deeply corrupt situation.

verses.text: It shall be that in the morning, as soon as the sun is up, you shall rise early and rush on the city. Behold, when he and the people who are with him come out against you, then may you do to them as you shall find occasion.”
verses.arminianNotes: Zebul tells him to rush the city at sunrise and deal with Gaal as he finds occasion. Arminian readers note the open-ended instruction, which leaves Abimelech free to act as harshly as he chooses against Shechem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the plan setting the stage for the fire Jotham foresaw coming out of Abimelech against Shechem. Shared ground: the verse closes the plotting and points toward the violent confrontation in the next section.
